books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, B. Debating the Future of Slavery in America

primary_sources: William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, 1831

stimulus.text: "On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation. . . . I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD." — William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, January 1, 1831
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from William Lloyd Garrison, "To the Public," The Liberator, January 1, 1831. Wording checked against the first-edition text as reprinted by Britannica and the LibreTexts edition; ellipses mark omissions.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Garrison, The Liberator (1831)
stem: Garrison's refusal to use "moderation" best illustrates which of the following positions?

options.text: Gradual emancipation, ending slavery over time
options.misconception: Gradualism is the moderate path; Garrison rejects moderation outright.

options.text: Colonization of free African Americans in Liberia
options.misconception: Colonization sends people away; Garrison demands freedom here, now.

options.text: Leaving slavery to be decided by each state
options.misconception: Leaving it to the states is a compromise; Garrison demands a national end to slavery.

rationales.A: Gradual emancipation would free slaves slowly, over generations. Garrison says he will not retreat a single inch, which is the opposite of gradual.
rationales.B: Colonization would send free Black people to Africa. Garrison's editorial demands freedom in America, not removal.
rationales.C: Garrison refuses moderation and vows to be heard. He wants slavery ended at once, with no payment to owners and equal rights for the freed.
rationales.D: Letting each state decide would leave slavery standing in the South. Garrison calls the whole nation to end it.
rationales.general:
1. Hear the vow. Garrison will not think, speak, or write with moderation about slavery.
2. Name what no moderation means. He will not accept delay, payment to owners, or removal to Africa.
3. Match the demand. Ending slavery at once, unpaid, is immediate emancipation.
Background: Garrison began publishing the Liberator in Boston on January 1, 1831.
Remember: when a reformer refuses moderation, ask which compromise he is refusing.
